Interior design client questionnaire

Begin with how the household lives, not with a shopping list. This client questionnaire separates everyday needs, preferences, practical constraints, and unanswered questions so the first meeting has a clear purpose.

By OpenLintel · Updated September 14, 2026 · Educational resource

Worked example & fields

Illustrative teaching extension of The Window Room. Pending review; not a client record, supplier quote, site survey, or construction-ready document.

Worked example preview · DOCX

Project and contact

Record the project reference, preferred contact channel, and property location in your private copy. Ask only for contact information you need.

The Window Room; illustrative example; no real client contact details.

Who uses the room?

Ask about routines, visitors, pets, changing household needs, and any access requirements the client wants to share.

Reading and conversation are the sample brief’s priorities. Household composition and access needs are not specified; confirm in discovery.

What works today?

Identify existing qualities worth keeping before discussing replacements.

Retain the existing oak floor; Keep the window and entrance positions; Bring reading, conversation, and storage into one room

What is difficult today?

Ask for specific moments: where belongings collect, when light is uncomfortable, or how activities compete.

The brief asks for reading, gathering, and storage to work together. Specific day-to-day frustrations still need a client conversation.

What should it feel like?

Request a few references and ask what the client likes about each: light, material, layout, or atmosphere. Do not assume they want every object shown.

Quiet Oak is the selected illustrative route: pale oak, warm mineral walls, and linen. Deep Olive remains a comparison study.

What must stay?

List retained objects and fixed conditions. Confirm dimensions and condition separately at survey.

Keep the existing oak floor, window position, and entrance position.

Budget and timing

Distinguish an overall allowance from design fees, purchasing, and installation. Record target dates and their reasons without promising feasibility.

Budget and installation dates are not established in the sample; record as open decisions.

Who decides, and what happens next?

Identify who consolidates feedback and how decisions will be recorded. Agree the next meeting and outstanding information.

Decision-maker not specified. Next step: confirm the brief and survey the room before developing selections.

How to use this template

Send the blank questionnaire before discovery, then review it together. Invite short answers and allow “not sure yet”; a missing answer is a follow-up task, not permission to assume. Store completed forms in your own secure project system, not on this website.

  1. Send the questions with a short explanation of how answers will be used.
  2. Discuss conflicting priorities in discovery; record questions rather than resolving them silently.
  3. Transfer agreed needs into the brief and assign follow-up information to an owner.

Review before use

  • Do not treat an inspiration image as a specification.
  • Do not convert an aspirational budget or date into a commitment.
  • Do not collect unnecessary sensitive household information.

Make it your own

Separate blank and worked-example documents. Edit the blank copy in Word or a compatible document editor.
